tier_reason: First-party README speedup tables (relative to PyTorch fp16 on A100) with no raw timings, no compiler or flags, no host CPU and no harness for those tables, so C. The README cites a NAACL-HLT 2021 industry paper and the LightSeq2 paper (search results say SC22), which could support B, but arxiv.org, aclanthology.org and the authors' site were all blocked here, so neither was opened.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README headline: up to 3x fp16 training vs PyTorch fp16, up to 5x int8 training vs PyTorch QAT, and up to 12x (fp16) and 15x (int8) inference vs PyTorch fp16. The README's own tables top out lower: fp16 training at 1.99x (Transformer, 512 tokens) and 2.12x (BERT, batch 8), int8 training 1.86x vs PyTorch fp16, which is about 5.2x vs PyTorch QAT at 0.36 (derived from page data); Transformer inference 11.82x fp16 and 14.44x int8 (batch 32, seq 8); BERT inference 1.82x fp16 and 2.04x int8 at batch 32, seq 128. docs/performance.md (T4, Transformer-base beam search): LightSeq is slower than FasterTransformer at batch 1 (29.66 vs 26.25 ms) and up to about 1.4x faster at batch 32 to 128; with sampling it is 0.85x to 1.40x of FasterTransformer.
corrections.caveats: First-party speedup ratios without raw timings, compiler, flags or host CPU, and the headline 'up to 3x' fp16 training is not supported by the README tables (maximum 2.12x). The baseline is eager PyTorch fp16, not a tuned path; against FasterTransformer on T4 (docs/performance.md) LightSeq is slower at batch 1 and with sampling at batch 128. The only public timing script found is examples/inference/python/test/ls_bert.py (one timed call vs Hugging Face), not the harness behind the tables. The repository was archived on 2025-07-21.

notes: Metadata confirmed on the GitHub page: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file), 3.3k stars, 333 forks, archived 2025-07-21, last commit 2023-05-10, latest release v3.0.0 (Oct 2022); abandoned is correct. Possible retier to B if a check can open the NAACL 2021 / LightSeq2 (SC22) papers.

tier_reason: First-party README plots (assets/peak.png, models.png, sustained.png) of speedup over FP16 PyTorch matmul on named GPUs, produced by the public bench.py. setup.py builds with torch CUDAExtension defaults and states no flags, and the host CPU is not stated, so it is not A. The paper was published at PPoPP '25 (per search results; ACM DOI 10.1145/3710848.3710871), which could support B, but every host serving it was blocked here.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Approximate plot readings (derived from page data). Peak plot (A10, 72k x 18k matrix, group size 128): Marlin about 3.87x to 3.9x over FP16 PyTorch at batch 1 to 16, 3.8x at 32, 3.1x at 64 and 1.55x at 128, tracking the 'Ideal' line; at batch 16, torch-nightly about 1.4x, exllamav2 about 0.7x, AWQ about 0.3x, bitsandbytes about 0.4x. Model layers at batch 16: about 3.4x to 4.25x on A10, 3090 and A6000, and 2.2x to 3.65x on A100. Sustained plot (A10 at locked base clock): about 3.9x to batch 16, 3.3x at 32, 1.7x at 64 and 1.0x at 128. README text: 'close to ideal (4x)' up to batch 16-32, with a maximum of 3.87x after the group-scale overhead.
corrections.hardware: NVIDIA A10 with ECC disabled (peak and sustained plots); A10, RTX 3090, A6000 and A100 (model layers); host CPU not stated; CUDA >= 11.8, torch >= 2.0
corrections.caveats: First-party README results shown only as plots; bench.py times 1 warmup and 10 iterations with time.time and deliberately does not synchronize between launches; setup.py uses torch CUDAExtension defaults and states no flags; host CPU not stated; ECC was disabled on the A10. The baseline is FP16 PyTorch matmul, labelled as calling CUTLASS. The headline compares 4-bit to 16-bit weights, so the speedup is the memory-traffic saving of weight quantisation (the 'Ideal' curve is 3.87x), not a faster FP16 kernel; it falls to about 1.55x at batch 128 (1.0x at locked base clock) and is lower on A100. The README cites arXiv 2408.11743; search results say the paper appeared at PPoPP '25, but it could not be opened here.

notes: Metadata confirmed on the GitHub page: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file), 1.2k stars, 93 forks, 14 commits, last commit 2024-09-04 ('Update README.md to point to arxiv paper'), not archived or a fork; stale. Search snippets of the paper abstract mention up to 2.8x end-to-end speedup inside vLLM. Retier to B is possible if a check can open the PPoPP '25 paper.

tier_reason: A single user's GitHub issue with raw benchmark output but no CPU model, compiler or flags; the XNNPACK baseline was run as 'bazel run //:convolution_bench' without '-c opt' (Bazel's default fastbuild, unoptimized), while XNNPACK's README builds its benchmarks with 'bazel build -c opt'. The rule for debug/-O0 baselines caps this at C, and the 40x-42x ratio is not a fair comparison.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Issue output: NNPACK (benchmark_conv, WT8x8 Winograd, 1 thread, 3 iterations) 31.948 ms and 76.170 ms (block multiplication 91.4 and 89.3 GFLOPS) vs XNNPACK convolution_bench 1345.8 ms and 3060.0 ms (7.07 and 7.05 GFLOPS, 1 iteration) for 256-to-128 channels at 128x128 and 192-to-96 channels at 256x256 with 3x3 kernels: about 42x and 40x (derived from page data). The XNNPACK run was most likely an unoptimized Bazel fastbuild (no '-c opt'), so the ratio overstates the gap; the reporter's own estimate on real networks is that XNNPACK was 3-5x slower on arm64 and x86, with no numbers given.
corrections.caveats: The only evidence is one user's June 2020 GitHub issue (Kepnu4), closed with no maintainer explanation visible; CPU model (6 cores at 4300 MHz, 9 MiB L3), compiler and flags are not stated. XNNPACK was run with 'bazel run //:convolution_bench' without '-c opt', i.e. Bazel's unoptimized fastbuild default (XNNPACK's README uses '-c opt'), which fits its 7 GFLOPS on a 4.2 GHz core. The second XNNPACK run reports Freq=1.18G under a CPU-scaling warning, and each XNNPACK case ran 1 iteration. NNPACK uses Winograd F(6x6,3x3) and XNNPACK direct convolution, so effective GFLOPS compare different algorithms. No commits since February 2023.
corrections.hardware: 6-core CPU at 4300 MHz, caches L1/L2/L3 32 KiB/256 KiB/9216 KiB (model not named), Ubuntu, single thread

notes: Downgraded for an overstated claim (tier stays C): the 40x-42x gap almost certainly reflects an unoptimized XNNPACK build. Metadata confirmed on the GitHub page: BSD-2-Clause (LICENSE file: Facebook / Georgia Tech), 1.7k stars, 321 forks, 374 commits, last commit 2023-02-01, not archived; abandoned is correct. Shortcoming to record: the baseline was likely unoptimized and there is no fair numeric evidence; a better numbers page would help (none found in the README).
